notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Speed signs say "Maximum" on one line and use km/h, so the numbers run higher than in the southern neighbour.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Signs lean on symbols: railway crossing and yield signs are blank, with no words.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Diamond-shaped T-junction signs exist in no other country.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Single yellow centre lines are usual, though doubles are fairly common too.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: British-style spelling in most places; Québec and parts of New Brunswick use a second official language, with bilingual signs elsewhere.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: A fair amount of Generation 2 coverage, especially rural and remote areas; Generation 3 is also far more common than in the south.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Communal mailboxes with a red postal logo are seen; they are very rare in the southern neighbour.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Short plates with a design unique to each province; several provinces skip front plates.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Wooden poles with large metal cylinder transformers and raised insulators: typical of North America.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: A green national trunk-highway shield is found in all 10 provinces.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Round white bollard wrapped by two black bands, found often at intersections. Bands can be yellow or blue in places.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: A bollard much like the Alberta one but with thicker black bands.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Thin, slightly curved black-and-white bollard, most common on Vancouver Island.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Black and grey painted bollards, usually with an orange stripe below; wooden rectangular ones in the far north.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Long thin white posts with a red or green reflector, always attached to guardrails.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Flat yellow bollards on the main trunk highway in New Brunswick.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Stop signs reading "Arrêt" are found only in Québec; signs with both words are most common in New Brunswick.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Red and white chevrons are used only in Québec; elsewhere they are yellow and black.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: T-junction signs in Québec lack the chequerboard pattern.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Newfoundland T-junction signs have a rectangular yellow border around the diamond.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Yellow fire hydrant markers sit on top of signposts in Québec.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Ontario kilometre markers have a white square at the bottom; some speed signs have a black strip reading km/h.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Sign backs are often green in British Columbia, and somewhat so on Prince Edward Island.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Alberta rural roads form a numbered grid of Township roads (east-west) and Range roads (north-south).

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Manitoba rural roads are numbered by grid with N, E or W letters.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Round wooden posts joined by exactly three metal wires, some with a white reflective band.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Wooden guardrail posts often have a pyramid-shaped top.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Concrete barriers are used far more than guardrails.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Pole tops with two side insulators and one on top, attached with a distinct bracket.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Pole-top insulators alternate: one left and two right, then two left and one right.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Transformers face the road in British Columbia and New Brunswick, and sit at 45 degrees in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Ontario uses orange and black striped traffic cones; Québec uses orange and white ones.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Flat, very sparsely populated prairie with farmland and few trees, drier toward the southwest.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Bright yellow canola fields in the central southern prairies.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Exposed bedrock of the great northern shield is common in the east.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Red-tinted soil and potato farming on Prince Edward Island.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: White-trunked aspen forests, turning bright yellow in fall, in the prairie provinces.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Dry hills with brown grassland and pine slopes around Kamloops and Kelowna.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Boreal hills with conifers that get thinner and shorter northward, often in Generation 2 coverage.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Tricolour flag with a yellow star on the blue band marks Acadian areas.
